Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

#7718. Three men charged in $130M AI impersonation scheme

Three foreign nationals are accused of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million. (Image from Shutterstock)

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan have unsealed an indictment accusing three foreign nationals of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million, according a story published Friday in The Guardian.

According to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit manipulated voices and images to deceive employees at companies around the world between 2024 and 2026. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain this summer, and Sheetrit was taken into custody in the United Kingdom in September.

According to prosecutors, the scheme worked in two stages. First, the defendants allegedly posed as a company executive and told employees they needed help with a confidential financial matter. Employees were then directed to contact attorneys at a major international law firm, whom the defendants also allegedly impersonated, and to wire large sums as instructed.

Prosecutors allege that the defendants stole nearly $5 million from a Missouri hospital system, about $2.7 million from a Rhode Island bank, roughly $3 million from a California hospital system, more than $4.6 million from a Massachusetts mutual fund, about $5 million from a Florida pet food company, and over $11 million from a U.K. technology company. The defendants have been indicted on charges relating to wire fraud, money laundering, conspiracy and identity theft.

Funds were allegedly routed to accounts in countries including the U.S., Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China, then converted to cryptocurrency to hide their origin and split among conspirators. Prosecutors say Soall and Hazan used several aliases, including “Rocky Balboa,” “Superman Cash” and “Ron.”

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement that while AI holds great promise, it can also be turned to criminal ends.

#7717. Justice Department Issues Fact Sheets About Lease Terminations for Servicemembers and their Dependents

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Justice Department announced today that it has issued two fact sheets to help servicemembers, including those who are returning to civilian life as veterans, avoid unnecessary rent payments and costly fees. The first explains how servicemembers and their dependents can end a residential or business lease on receiving eligible military orders. And the second explains how they can end certain vehicle leases.

“The Civil Rights Division is deeply committed, on Veterans Day and every other day, to ensuring that our military families are not saddled with excessive fees and payments as they heroically serve our country,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Jesus A. Osete of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “These fact sheets are an important reminder for the military community, and to vehicle lenders and landlords, that servicemembers and their families have a legal right to end certain leases early when they transition to veteran status or are called to move on military orders.”

Military families are often required to relocate through a process known as “Permanent Change of Station” (PCS) moves. Because of the frequency of these moves, servicemembers are likely to end up in leases that need to be terminated early. The Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA) allows servicemembers to cancel these leases so that they are not stuck paying for a residence or vehicle that they can no longer use solely because they are moving in service for our country.

The Department is issuing these fact sheets near Veterans Day to draw attention to an important part of the lease termination right: retirement and separation orders are eligible military orders for lease termination. When a servicemember transitions into veteran status, they receive a retirement or separation order that shows they are leaving military service. Lease holders and landlords may not recognize that these orders are covered by the SCRA, since they are not the typical PCS orders. But military families often use retirement or separation to relocate, and not recognizing these orders would leave them paying for a residence or vehicle that they may no longer need.

Our veterans face significant challenges when leaving military service. Recognizing these rights can spare these military families a large financial burden at a time of significant transition.

The Servicemembers and Veterans Initiative, housed in the Department’s Civil Rights Division, works to ensure that the rights of the brave men and women of our nation’s armed forces, and the veterans who have served in the past, are safeguarded from discrimination and unfair treatment.

The Department’s enforcement of the SCRA is conducted by the Civil Rights Division’s Housing and Civil Enforcement Section in partnership with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country. Since 2011, the Department has obtained over $490 million in monetary relief for over 153,000 servicemembers through its enforcement of the SCRA. For more information about the Department’s enforcement efforts under the SCRA and other laws that protect the rights of servicemembers and their families, please visit www.servicemembers.gov.

Servicemembers, veterans, and their dependents who believe that their rights under the SCRA have been violated should contact the nearest Armed Forces Legal Assistance Program Office. Office locations may be found at legalassistance.law.af.mil. If servicemembers, veterans, or their spouses are not eligible for military legal assistance services, they may request that the Justice Department review their claim by submitting a complaint through civilrights.justice.gov/.

#7715. Art, syrup, a legendary stone: Maxie Dara’s 3 favorite heists of the last century

Crime is a subject often synonymous with tragedy, with strife, with human suffering. But sometimes it’s also a little goofy.

I spent my first two books, A Grim Reaper’s Guide to Catching a Killer and A Grim Reaper’s Guide to Cheating Death, focused on the murder of it all. My search history probably has me on at least one watch list and I can give you a handful of creative ways to kill somebody with a glitter pen if you ask nicely.

But for my third dive back into my world of death with A Grim Reaper’s Guide to Living Twice, I decided to play against type and go for a silly little heist instead. And it turns out I’m not alone. It fact, it turns out recent history is full of silly little heists that take the concept of a crime and turn it into a certified shenanigan. From student hijinks to condiment capers, here are my top three favorite heists of the last century.

Come with me to my home nation of Canada, to my birth province of Quebec, where poutine is plentiful and everybody’s at least a little disappointed in your lack of French fluency. It also happens to be a hub of maple syrup production, though that feels like something of an understatement. According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, “In 2020, Quebec contributed 96.4 per cent of Canadian maple product exports.”

With all that sweet tree nectar flowing, it may come as no surprise to you (though it genuinely did to me) to learn that the province keeps a syrup stockpile in the form of the Strategic Maple Syrup Reserve. Think of it as a sort of Fort Knox, but instead of gold it’s filled with pancake toppings, which is way more appealing in my opinion. And I’m not the only one who thinks so.

Between 2011 and 2012, a group of sticky-fingered (sorry) Reserve employees decided to help themselves to the stock in order to sell it to other provinces and states. This slow-motion heist involved months of siphoning maple syrup out of heavy barrels. The thieves would then either replace their loot with water or leave the barrels empty. Unfortunately for the robbers, there’s a bit of a difference between an empty barrel and one filled with syrup—a six-hundred-pound difference, in fact.

When an inspector for the organization in charge of the Reserve tried to climb up a stack of these supposedly heavy barrels only for one to nearly topple under his weight, he became just a smidge suspicious. Sure enough, a subsequent investigation found that around three thousand tonnes of maple syrup had been stolen, its value a staggering $18 million.

The investigation also uncovered a crime ring comprised of syrup industry insiders, from truck drivers to sugar shack workers, who had rented a separate space in the same warehouse as the Reserve so they could perpetrate their crimes unnoticed. Though my favourite fact about this entire case is that a maple syrup black market exists, and the ringleader of the operation, Richard Vallières, had already been a part of it long before this heist. Some criminal underworlds just sound more delicious than others, you know?

Kids these days, with their music and their haircuts and their schemes to steal back ancient symbols of Scottish heritage.

It’s Christmas in 1950 and four Glasgow University students have decided to crank their youthful rebellion up a notch. While other twenty-somethings are sleeping off hangovers or opening presents with their families, Ian Hamilton, Gavin Vernon, Kay Matheson and Alan Stuart are plotting to retrieve the Stone of Scone.

Also known as the Stone of Destiny, the roughly three-hundred-and-thirty-six-pound block of red sandstone had been an important part of Scottish coronations for hundred of years before King Edward I stole it for England during the 13th century. During its long history the stone was imbued with rich legends, connecting its heritage all the way back to the first king of Scotland and making it an important national symbol. South of the border it continued to be used in coronations, this time siting beneath each English monarch as they were crowned, but its importance to Scotland remained.

Centuries after its initial theft by King Edward I, the four plucky students decided to reclaim the stone in an act of national pride. The group drove south and waited until midnight to steal the Stone of Scone from where it now lay in Westminster Abbey.

With Kay on guard duty, the three men tried to hoist the stone to freedom, but it broke in two during their attempt. Ian took the smaller piece while Gavin and Alan took the larger and fled in a separate car. Back with Kay, Ian soon found himself in the crosshairs of a passing officer, but in an Ocean’s Eleven-like twist, the students disguised their heist as a youthful makeout session and managed to get away.

The story only gets more wild from there, with the stone halves finding themselves hidden under floorboards and buried under a campsite before they were eventually reunited. And while it did end up returning to England after the students were caught, the Stone of Scone was given back to Scotland in 1996, and none of the young thieves faced legal consequences for their actions.

The Louvre is no stranger to an entertaining heist. In 1911, a man called Vincenzo Peruggia dressed as a museum worker and snatched the Mona Lisa in broad daylight. Unfortunately for the Louvre but very fortunately for schadenfreude fans everywhere, the museum art minister was on holiday at the time and before he left he had apparently insisted, “don’t call me unless the Louvre burns down or the Joconde [French for Mona Lisa] is stolen.”

Fast forward just shy of a hundred years and this same level of absolute tomfoolery was on display again. In 2025, two men dressed as construction workers, hoisted themselves up to a museum balcony using a furniture lift and stole €88 million worth of French Crown Jewels in under eight minutes. Though the culprits were eventually caught, the heist will live on in infamy for both its devious efficiency and the frankly top tier memes it inspired.

Maxie Dara is a writer and actor from Ontario, Canada. She has been a freelance journalist focusing on the local arts and culture scene for more than five years, with bylines in publications such as Hamilton Magazine and Beyond James, among others. She is also a two-time award-winning playwright, taking home the Best of Fringe award at the 2017 Hamilton Fringe Festival for the musical comedy This Is Not a Musical: The Musical! and the 2020 Torpedo Prize for her play Alone Together, a pandemic drama. Maxie knew she wanted to be a writer at the age of seven, when she first fell in love with the written word. She also wanted to be a mermaid but has mostly focused on the writing side of things.

#7714. The Queens Public Library system is being held for ransom

In a bizarre turn of events, on Wednesday November 4th, New York City’s Queens Public Library (QPL)  system (which operates 66 branches), experienced an attack on its online networks by a hacker. The entire system is offline, and is being held for ransom.

According to the QPL, all branches remain open, but online networks are down, resulting in disruptions to the library website, on-site computers, check-out and return machines, wi-fi, the library’s mobile app, and all digital media services.

It has not been disclosed what or how much the hackers are asking in return for releasing the system. It is also unknown who is behind the ransomware attack.

QPL CEO Dennis Walcott told Gothamist, “Unfortunately, it’s part of the world that we live in right now. So the Queens Public Library is a victim of the type of world that we’re living in, where people are launching cyber attacks against various types of entities, large corporations, and now Queens Public Library.”

His remark highlights the absolute strangeness of the events… the QPL is hardly a “large corporation.” In fact, it’s a very small nonprofit. It’s not even New York’s largest library system. The NYPL, which services Manhattan, the Bronx, and Staten Island, operates 92 locations. (For those wondering, the Brooklyn Public Library system operates 62 branches.)

But also… it’s a library system! It’s whole business is to provide widespread access to books, additional literary and media resources, internet access, printing services, education opportunities, and community and children’s programming to people. FOR FREE. What the hell type of jerk goes after a library system, especially a library system in one of the most ethnically and linguistically diverse areas in the world? (As a Queens native and huge QPL fan, but also just a person who thinks books are good, I’m furious.)

Walcott also noted that it is currently unknown if user information has been compromised.

However, QPL users can still check books in and out manually (it is a library, after all). So, analog tech has saved the day.

Stay tuned for more updates, and long live libraries!

#7712. Will an ability to hold federal officers accountable survive this term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

At a time when there is a desire to hold ICE agents accountable for their constitutional violations, the Supreme Court might be poised to eliminate the only way to hold them civilly liable under federal law.

By way of background, if state or local officers violate the Constitution, they can be sued under a federal statute, 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. But no federal law authorizes suits against federal officers for constitutional violations. Rather, the ability to sue a federal government officer for money damages comes from a 1971 Supreme Court decision, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. There, the court said that it would allow a cause of action for money damages under the Fourth Amendment even without a federal statute authorizing it.

Nevertheless, for decades, the Supreme Court has refused to extend or even apply Bivens to other violations of constitutional rights by federal officers, and several conservative justices have called for it to be overruled. Now, in Nielsen v. Watanabe, to be argued on Nov. 9, the court will again confront whether to allow a Bivens suit – and perhaps whether to end such claims entirely.

The underlying issue is about separation of powers: should the court provide a remedy for constitutional violations or is that entirely the province of Congress? But it also is about accountability: without Bivens, how can those who violate constitutional rights, including ICE agents, be held responsible and how can those injured be compensated?

Webster Bivens alleged that he had been subjected to an illegal and humiliating search by agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. Bivens sought money damages as compensation for the harms he suffered. The court held that a federal law cause of action for money damages could be inferred directly from the Fourth Amendment. The majority, in an opinion by Justice William Brennan, emphasized that individuals whose rights have been violated should not be relegated to state law remedies, which might be inadequate or hostile to the federal constitutional interest.

In an important and often-cited concurring opinion, Justice John Marshall Harlan explained that the federal courts long have devised remedies for violations of federal law. Harlan said that it is essential that federal courts be able to provide such relief because “it is apparent that some form of damages is the only possible remedy for someone in Bivens’ alleged position. … For people in Bivens’ shoes, it is damages or nothing.” Harlan rejected the claim that the court violates separation of powers when it creates such a cause of action and remedy. In his view, the court is responsible for upholding and enforcing the Bill of Rights, and, hence, the judiciary need not wait for the legislature in order to act.

Chief Justice Warren Burger and Justices Hugo Black and Harry Blackmun dissented. Each wrote an opinion arguing that separation of powers means that Congress, and not the court, should create a cause of action for damages against federal officers. Black explained that “[s]hould the time come when Congress desires such lawsuits, it has before it a model of valid legislation, 42 U.S.C. §1983, to create a damage remedy against federal officers.” Similarly, Blackmun argued that “it is the Congress, and not this Court, that should act.”

For a decade after Bivens, the court applied and extended it. In 1979’s Davis v. Passman, the court allowed a Bivens suit under the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment for an equal protection claim. Congressman Otto Passman fired his administrative assistant, Shirley Davis, because he wanted a male to fill the position. In allowing the suit against the congressman, the court emphasized the judiciary's role in ensuring effective protection of constitutional rights.

And only a year later, in Carlson v. Green, the court allowed a Bivens suit for violation of the Eighth Amendment. A mother sued federal prison officials on behalf of her deceased son, claiming that he was the victim of gross inadequacies of medical facilities and staff, which caused his death and constituted cruel and unusual punishment. A remedy was available under the Federal Tort Claims Act; thus, the issue before the court was whether a Bivens suit should be allowed in light of this alternative. The court concluded that Bivens suits were a “counterpart” to the Federal Tort Claims Act because the act creates liability for the federal government and a Bivens cause of action permits recovery from federal officers themselves. The court found no indication that Congress intended for the act to preclude Bivens suits.

Since 1980, however, the court has not ruled in favor of a Bivens claim. In its most recent decision about Bivens, 2022’s Egbert v. Boule, the court noted that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.”

Specifically, the court has held that that such claims are not allowed if there is a statute that precludes suits (in 2010’s Hui v. Castaneda), or that provides an alternative remedy even if it is inadequate (in 1988’s Schweiker v. Chilicky). It has precluded Bivens claims for those injured while in the military, even for egregious violations of their rights (in 1987’s United States v. Stanley). It has ruled that Bivens suits should be allowed only if they are on balance desirable and consistently has found that they are not (in 2007’s Wilkie v. Robbins, 2017’s Ziglar v. Abbasi, 2020’s Hernandez v. Mesa, and Boule). And it has precluded Bivens suits against private prisons that contract with the federal government (in 2001’s Correctional Services Corp. v. Malesko) and the guards employed by them (in 2012’s Minecci v. Pollard).

Based on this line of cases, the court in Egbert v. Boule stressed that recognizing a Bivens cause of action “is ‘a disfavored judicial activity.’” The court stated that

The court then laid out the framework for Bivens claims going forward. According to the majority, this should be guided by a two-step inquiry:

This is a test that puts a very strong presumption against recognizing Bivens claims.

Like Carlson v. Green, Nielsen v. Watanabe involves an Eighth Amendment claim for cruel and unusual punishment.The case involves a prisoner, Kekai Watanabe, who alleges that he suffered a broken tailbone when attacked by other prisoners that caused him excruciating pain and that a staff nurse, Francis Nielsen, denied him medical care. The court granted review as to whether the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit “erred [here] in recognizing a Bivens cause of action.”

Watanabe argues to the court that this case is governed by Carlson v. Green and does not seek to extend Bivens in any way. His brief states: “Watanabe asserts the same kind of violation of the same constitutional right by the same type of defendant in the same institutional setting pursuant to the same substantive standards as the plaintiff in Carlson. This is precisely the kind of claim this Court has long understood Carlson to encompass.”

In response, Nielsen argues that Bivens suits are strongly disfavored and that there are “significant factual differences such as the immediacy and severity of the harm alleged” compared with Carlson. But that is not all: Nielsen also expressly argues that “Bivens should be overruled” and that “Congress, not the judiciary, creates causes of action.”

The court could affirm the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit and allow a Bivens suit, saying that this is governed by Carlson. Or the court could distinguish Carlson, accepting Nielsen’s argument that there are sufficient factual differences between the cases, essentially limiting Bivens claims only for cruel and unusual punishment claims involving deaths. Or the court could overrule Carlson but not overrule Bivens.

Or the court could overrule Bivens entirely, which several conservative justices have advocated in the past.

The fundamental disagreement, as it was in Bivens, is whether it is the judicial role to provide remedies for violations of constitutional rights or whether that is just for Congress. The practical reality is that without Bivens suits, those whose rights have been violated – even horribly – are left with no recourse. In Hernandez v. Mesa, for example, a boy in Mexico was killed by shot fired across the border by a federal agent in Texas. The court’s rejection of a Bivens suit left no remedy at all.

In that case, and in many other situations, the Federal Tort Claims Act does not allow suits against the United States. Often there are not state tort remedies available either. To paraphrase Justice Harlan, for people in the shoes of many injured by federal officers, it is Bivens suits or nothing.

I would like to think that the reports of egregious constitutional violations by ICE agents, including killings, would cause the court to realize the importance of Bivens suits and to not end such causes of action. That is what makes Nielsen v. Watanabe so important.

Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

#7709. Of mistletoe and murder: 7 holiday mysteries set in the past

Mysteries set during the weeks leading up to Christmas are some of my favorites, and I know I’m hardly alone in loving a good holiday read. There’s just something about the sights and sounds of merriment juxtaposed with the increasingly dark and cold nights that make for a mystery that is that much more fun than one set in any other time of the year.

This is especially true for historical mysteries, in my opinion. For instance, in Murder of a Merry Gentleman, the fourth installment of my Lady Petra Inquires series set in Regency-era England, I set the mystery of a bachelor gentleman’s death in the ballroom of the famed Almack’s Assembly Rooms during the fortnight (i.e., two weeks) before Christmas.

Possibly helped by the lack of modern technology, sometimes the absence of modern lighting, and occasionally the dangers of period-correct clothing, all the little contradictions that give a mystery with a Christmastime setting such an fascinating ambience made it all the more fun for me to write, and I think makes holiday whodunits set in the past all the more enjoyable to read.

Here are seven historical mysteries I’ve especially loved that are all set during the holidays, where the festive season gives as much to the whodunit as the plot, no matter what the time period.

Setting: New York, 1932.  After Grace Verlander, the assistant who keeps Macy’s department store running smoothly, receives a note from Santa Claus that claims he’s been sent a death threat, she ramps up security around the annual Thanksgiving Day Parade. Yet when a dead body turns up on a parade float, Grace must use all the secrets she knows about the store to help uncover a killer and keep Macy’s reputation shining.

Rhys Bowen, The Twelve Clues of Christmas (Her Royal Spyness, book 6)

Setting: Scotland and England, 1933.  When Lady Georgie escapes the dreadfully cold Scottish winter to help play hostess at a holiday party in the village of Tiddleton-under-Lovey, she doesn’t expect a series of murders to be part of the season. And when they start following the theme of a well-known Christmas carol, it’s up to Georgie to find the culprit before the twelve days turn even more tragic.

Jess Armstrong, The Devil in Oxford (Ruby Vaughn mysteries, book 3)

Setting:  Oxford, England, 1922. American heiress Ruby Vaughn is hoping to spend a quiet Christmas in Oxford when she reluctantly agrees to accompany her octogenarian employer, Mr. Owen, to an antiquities exhibition with a mysterious past.

But when the discredited scholar who collected the artifacts turns up dead, and an old friend of Ruby’s asks for her help, Ruby will be pulled into an investigation into the dark world of antiquities that may turn out to be more dangerous than she ever imagined.

Dianne Freeman, A Christmas Guide to Family and Murder (Countess of Harleigh mysteries, book 9)

Setting:  Norfolk, England, 1900. Frances Hazelton—the American-born and widowed Countess of Harleigh—and her still-new husband George travel to the Norfolk estate of her sister-in-law Fiona to enjoy the Christmas holiday.

Yet when the aftermath of a terrible storm finds the local (and possibly disreputable) doctor dead in a nearby field, Frances and Fiona will unearth many a secret in their quest to find a killer and restore the Christmas spirit to both her family and the local village.

James R. Benn, The Phantom Patrol (A Billy Boyle WWII mystery, book 19)

Setting: Paris, 1944. With France only recently liberated, Captain Billy Boyle, and former Boston cop working as a special investigator for General Eisenhower, is sent to Paris. After discovering a rare piece of art and connecting it to a French network of Nazi sympathizers and art smugglers who might be aided by a member of the British Army, Billy races to hunt down the culprit, taking him directly to the frontlines of the Ardennes Forest and what will be come the deadly Battle of the Bulge.

Katharine Schellman, Murder at Midnight (Lily Adler mysteries, book 4)

Setting: Hertfordshire, England, 1816.  When widow Lily Adler visits the family of her late husband in Hertfordshire for Christmas, she finds herself reunited with her friend Captain Jack Hartley and his younger sister, Amelia, who has recently become the subject of scandalous gossip.

When a wealthy gentleman is found dead after a snowstorm, it’s Amelia who is suspected, and it’s up to Lily to uncover the truth and clear Amelia’s name before the girl’s reputation is tarnished forever.

Charles Finch, The Fleet Street Murders (Charles Lenox mysteries, Book 3)

Setting: London, 1866.  Christmas for gentleman sleuth Charles Lenox means celebrating his engagement to his dear friend Lady Jane. That is, until the murders of two journalists brings Lenox into a new investigation, and a secret is revealed that casts doubt on his future with his fiancée.

As he splits his time between London and the northern town of Stirrington, where he is running for Parliament, Lenox is drawn into a complex case that mixes politics and murder, bringing death and danger closer to home than ever before.

Celeste Connally is the USA Today bestselling author of the Lady Petra Inquires series, an Agatha Award nominee, and a former freelance writer and editor. Her mysteries are set in Regency-era England and feature a headstrong heroine, a feminist spin, and as many equestrian scenes as her plots and editor will allow. She delights in giving her mysteries a good dose of romance, too, and a few research facts she hopes you’ll find as interesting as she does. Passionate about history and slightly obsessed with period dramas, what Celeste loves most is reading and writing about women who don’t always do as they are told.

#7707. Virginia Trench on psychological thrillers and the dark sides of motherhood

There were ear-splitting screams. Bites. Lies of all shapes and sizes. Existential crises. And, it goes without saying, a lot of blood. Motherhood has all the raw materials for a good thriller.

Certainly not me—I was about to get a crash course, though. I was blissfully unaware of just how real my work would become once I had a newborn and second-degree tear in tow. I never expected to bring some of the most visceral aspects of my work home with me. But when my daughter arrived, all that went out the window.

From the moment we left the hospital, both of us exhausted, well out of our depth, and wearing diapers, something felt broken in me. (The baby, to be clear, was absolutely perfect).

I, by contrast, was nothing like the serene, softly smiling, well-lit mothers of Instagram. I felt more like a light-averse creature sharing more in common with feral raccoon than a human woman. I craved everything I couldn’t have: silence, rest, solitude, the home phone number of the anesthesiologist who messed up my epidural. A girl can dream—a mother can just tough it out.

As our new reality set in, everything I’d ever heard about motherhood started to seem like an elaborate, generations-long lie. But then, I reasoned, that couldn’t be the case. Surely, I must be the ugly, defective exception to the rule that childbirth and motherhood are the most beautiful, natural things in the world.

I gritted my teeth and waited for a switch to flip. Not not fantasizing about smashing the rocking swing with the annoying music, I did my best to fake it. I was desperate for the *alleged* biologically hardwired maternal peace to settle over us, to give my daughter the mother she deserved…and to prove the lactation consultant wrong—I wasn’t already failing because I’d given up on breastfeeding pretty much immediately.

Goodbye, Instagram moms. Hello, Nightbitch.

Sleepless night after shapeless day into the next sleepless night, I sank into a quicksand isolation, anger, and panic that came in bone-deep waves. Sure, I’d heard of postpartum depression, courtesy of delicately worded waiting room posters. I’d heard of the “baby blues,” a term was popularized by a man decades before American women could open their own bank accounts, receive paid maternity leave, or easily access contraception.

This experience was something else entirely, something huge, hungry, and raw. I used to love exploring those dark corners of human psychology. Through fiction, it was safe, easy to do from a creative distance. But that distance had vanished, and I found myself submerged in the extreme emotions that fuel stories I had no desire to live firsthand. The more I tried to escape those feelings, to remind myself how lucky I was and of the many privileges I have, the thicker my haze of shame became.

Out of sheer desperation, I tried something that seemed a little crazy at the time, even for a woman who heard phantom baby cries everywhere she went, including an empty Target bathroom. I evicted The Happiest Baby on the Block from my nightstand and replaced it with Rachel Yoder’s Nightbitch.

I faced the scary, socially unacceptable thoughts head-on. I nodded vigorously as I read. I started writing again. I gave voice to the emotional exhaust that followed me around like a swarm of black flies. And little by little, this brought me back from the brink.

In those pages, I finally, finally, found someone willing to level with me about the dark side of mothering.

As I tore through Yoder’s novel, I breathed in the unflinching honesty like fresh air. And after what I can only describe as the most isolated period of my life (despite rarely being alone), I could have lifted up Nightbitch like Simba in the Lion King.

To some, a twisted tale of rage and supernatural transformation might seem like an odd place to look for someone who gets you. Those people probably haven’t had to catch tiny human vomit with their bare hands or scrape diaper material from under their fingernails. For me, it was healing. It was therapy for the price of a hardcover—that eventually led to actual therapy. It was someone else, okay, fine, a fictional character, but still, validating everything so much of the world seems determined to silence.

Nightbitch was the gateway to more dark tales. It became an unexpected path back to a part of myself that got lost somewhere in the process of creating life and nesting the crap out of the former guest room. More than that, once I started reading thrillers again, I did so with new, narrowed eyes.

Psychological thrillers are a powerful channel for female rage, and the mom of it all adds fascinating layers to that rage. It’s hard not to occasionally lose your shit when (almost) everything is your fault.

Freudian psychology, direct ancestor of the manosphere, if you ask me, laid the groundwork to blame mothers for the behaviors and even the crimes of their children—especially their sons. We wonder: if a serial killer had just been nurtured properly, might innocent lives have been spared? Culture-defining classics from Psycho to Carrie feature the consequences of dangerous mothering, and audiences point the proverbial finger accordingly.

For that matter, is there anything more frightening than a bad mother? Sharp Objects and Verity terrify readers not just because of their villains’ psychosis, but their fundamental wrongness, their choice to harm, rather than nurture. That goes against nature, doesn’t it? After all, violence is supposed to be a man’s thing, isn’t it?

Most (all?) maternal attributes are fair game. A demanding career? Lack of career outside the home? An only child? Four under four? Homemade gluten free snacks? A Costco multipack or Cheez-Its?

Nothing is safe. All that pressure is enough to make anyone snap. And in this genre, that’s a great place to start.

Open Best Offer Wins, All the Other Mothers Hate Me, or Little Fires Everywhere, and we see death by a thousand little judgmental cuts, some of which are self-inflicted by the main characters. And as their stories unfold, we can’t look away.

Because instead of simply swallowing the judgement and striving to meet those double standards, these women make all hell break loose. And, as I can attest, there’s something cathartic about seeing that happen on the page. Many mothers have met their version of Renate Kline, for instance, ultra-judgmental supermom of Big Little Lies, and we can’t very well face off in real life and tell her exactly what we think of her, so it’s all the more satisfying to watch Reese Witherspoon do it for us in the TV adaptation.

It’s no wonder this genre draws in so many readers—we can relate to the characters’ experiences, ideally minus the murders.

If a “right” formula for this, it has eluded me completely. Too much hinges on who did/didn’t sleep through the night, which appliances are whistling at me, and whether my three-year-old is in a self-declared Aurora/ Ariel or Maleficent/ Ursula mood. So, I gave up looking, and I’m a much happier, better writer for it.

But I will tell you one thing: it helps to not have photos of my children in my office, and I feel zero guilt about this. Do I have a framed tooth in honor of the twist in Sharp Objects? A black and white portrait of Agatha Christie? Also, yes. But no adorable kids, and that’s okay, especially when I’m drafting a murderous chase scene.

It probably sounds corny: but the literal separation was necessary, even if my home office is feet away from the nursery. The best I can do is give make the space I can for different facets of my identity, which now includes, but is not eclipsed by, motherhood. Sometimes that space feels tiny, like hiding the last Annie’s Bunny Cracker bag for myself to pair with a glass of pinot noir.

Sometimes it feels huge, the inspiration for entire second novel, for instance, in all its raw, unfiltered glory (plus one sociopathic con man). What could go wrong?

Virginia Trench is the author of Our Secrets Were Safe. She studied English at Vanderbilt University before earning an MA in secondary education at University of Colorado Boulder. When she’s not writing, she can be found exploring the Rocky Mountains, struggling on a yoga mat while her cat judges her, or devouring the latest crime novels. She lives in Colorado with her family.

#7706. Former U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information and Stealing Night Vision Goggles

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private company that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7705. Idaho Man Sentenced to 18 Years in Prison for Attempting to Provide Material Support to ISIS in Plot to Attack Churches

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, was sentenced today to 18 years in prison and lifetime supervised release by U.S. District Judge David C. Nye of the District of Idaho for attempting to provide material support and resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

According to court records, Mercurio planned to incapacitate his father with a metal pipe and take his firearms to use in a mass casualty attack on Idaho churches in the name of ISIS. Mercurio also planned to use flame-covered weapons, explosives, knives, and a machete in the attacks. A search of his house revealed that he had butane canisters, lighters, a pair of handcuffs, a knife, and a machete, as well as several firearms belonging to his father. Days before the planned attack, Mercurio stood before an ISIS flag holding a knife and pledged his allegiance to ISIS. The FBI arrested him on April 6, 2024, one day before his planned attack. In addition to his plot to attack Idaho churches, in early 2023, he created an online repository for pro-ISIS content with the purpose of spreading the doctrine of the Islamic State.

“America’s founders wanted our Nation to be a place where the faithful of any denomination could exercise their religious beliefs freely and without fear of violence,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Alexander Scott Mercurio planned to attack that fundamental freedom by bringing death and destruction to several churches. This sentence shows that the Department of Justice will relentlessly investigate, pursue, and prosecute those who would terrorize and murder Americans for exercising their religious rights.”

“The sentencing of Mercurio today sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States – whether in Coeur d’Alene, or any other community – they will be brought to justice,” said U.S. Attorney John C. Shirts for the District of Idaho. “Protecting our communities from terrorist activity is always the number one priority of this office and the Department of Justice. I commend the investigation by the FBI, as well as the valuable assistance provided by the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.”

“With today’s sentencing, this individual is being held accountable for pledging allegiance to ISIS and planning an attack on U.S. soil,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI works tirelessly to detect and prevent acts of terrorism in order to protect the American people. We will continue to work closely with our law enforcement and Justice Department partners to make sure anyone who participates in terrorist acts faces justice.”

The case was investigated by the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force with assistance from the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Heather S. Patricco and David G. Robins for the District of Idaho and Trial Attorney Matthew R. Hracho of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7704. On Mole Men and Other Inspirations

I’d heard about the mole people living in the tunnels under Manhattan. But I only thought about them a few times a day, tops. Did they all carry flashlights, I wondered, or had their eyes evolved to pierce the perpetual subterranean night? Were rats a delicacy with the right recipe, or more of a utility feed for on-the-go snacking? Did a mole man’s skin become increasingly translucent, like certain shrimp, the deeper you went down?

Some questions will remain forever unanswered. As humans, we’re all piloted by this great mystery inside our heads. That’s something I thought about often while writing my novel Middleman. In an uncertain world, the main character seeks clarity and connection to the real thing, as he struggles to make peace with the never knowing. That sense of the never knowing felt especially vast when I was in my early twenties, twenty years ago, and included countless topics, mole people among them.

And then one night, I was waiting on the A train for a while. Long enough to sit down on a bench, though I had no disinfectant. I occupied myself with my notebook, writing my little things as I do, until I looked up to see if a subway was coming. What I saw instead was the silhouette of a hunched figure in the tunnel moving toward me. The handful of people waiting there all appeared distracted by their iPods and glossy magazines. We’re pretty good as a species at putting the blinders on.

But the woman sitting next to me on the bench did notice. She said, in a horrified whisper, “What is that?”

I had an idea, though I was too spooked to speak. The figure had a slight limp, but then as it entered the dim light of the station, it quickly pulled itself up onto the platform with impressive agility. It was a short man with a tangled gray beard, but most surprising was his attire. He was dressed almost entirely in bright green. Green pointy shoes even and a green felt cap with a little red feather. It sounds too cartoonish to be real, I know, but it’s true. I’d pass a lie detector test telling you that this mole man was dressed like Robin Hood. And not the Kevin Costener version. The original Howard Pyle one, the Disney one, the very green fella.

I was still new to the city then, but I’d learned already what every bumpkin must learn there, which is: you don’t have to engage with everyone, or anyone for that matter. Mind your own business and the person on the street with arrows sticking out of his back will move on, and you can go back to your eggs benedict. There are just too many people all at once, and you have to protect yourself from some of these wildcards, unless you want to suffer a lukewarm breakfast, or worse.

So, I didn’t make eye contact, as the guy got closer. I busied myself counting my shoes—one, and oh, look, there’s another one. This strategy didn’t work. He came right up to me and looked at my notebook. He gave a faint nod. I don’t recall exchanging any pleasantries. I just remember him saying, his voice gravelly, these words exactly: “If you ever run into trouble in the tunnels, tell ‘em you know Hobbit.”

Life is strange. And frightening. And funny. A lot of things can happen out there.

It didn’t occur to me until this very moment that maybe he was supposed to be dressed like a hobbit from L0rd of the Rings, and not Robin Hood, after all. Either way, he was living a cosplay fantasy life in the presumably dangerous underground. And after delivering his message to me and me alone, he turned and went back down the platform, climbed onto the tracks, and vanished again into the subway tunnel. That was it.

The woman next to me on the bench had taken off wisely before he limped up, and so I sat there alone wondering: What kind of unexpected turns would my life have to take to lead me into the tunnels? And who was the them, in Hobbit’s scenario, that might be giving me trouble down there? And how dire and desperate would my situation have to be to have just one card left to play, and it’s: name-dropping a mole man named Hobbit?

Life is strange. And frightening. And funny. A lot of things can happen out there. And this memory of Hobbit returned to me as I was writing the ne’er-do-well character, Eddie, in my book. Eddie doesn’t do any of the things a respectable adult is supposed to do. He doesn’t work, doesn’t have a family, doesn’t properly take care of his sick mother. He’s selfish, unscrupulous, and also, he’s enviably free, in his way.

He doesn’t compromise himself and he has the courage to pursue his own vision, however warped and misguided it may be, into the mausoleums of an old cemetery, a scary place for most people even in daylight. Perhaps almost as scary as the dark tunnels under Manhattan, where Hobbit went to an extreme to turn his fantasy life into his real one.

It feels fitting to me now that someone who lived like that would offer a young aspiring writer his protection, his blessing even maybe. And maybe someday I’ll be brave enough to follow him all the way down.

Brendan Flaherty is from outside Hartford. He went to Washington University in St. Louis, and received his MFA from Boston University. He lives with his wife and two sons. The Dredge is his debut novel.

#7703. Court seems poised to side with Catholic preschools in religious discrimination dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared ready to hold that the exclusion of Catholic preschools in Colorado from the state’s universal preschool program violates the First Amendment. After just over two hours of oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a majority seemed to agree with the challengers that Colorado’s refusal to provide them with an exemption from rules that would require the preschools to admit all students – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents – should be subject to a more stringent constitutional test than that applied by the lower court. The court could decide to apply that standard itself or send the case back to the lower courts for them to do so.

Colorado launched the universal preschool program, which provides families in the state with up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools, in 2023. To participate in the program, preschools must meet a variety of state standards and sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” The preschools cannot decline to serve LGBTQ families, because Colorado believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs – the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children – went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy. They contended that requiring Catholic preschools to agree to the nondiscrimination agreement to participate in the universal preschool program constitutes unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to carve out a religious exemption that allows them to take part in the program.

After both the district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the challengers’ claim, they came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to take up the case – which the court agreed in April 2026 to do.

Representing the challengers, Nicholas Reaves told the justices that the schools in the Archdiocese of Denver “exist to pass on the faith to the next generation.” “[T]his is not a zero-sum game,” he said, because “letting Catholic schools” participate in the universal preschool program “will create more seats for everyone.”

Representing the state, Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton countered that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools to” the program and allows them to teach their religious beliefs. It simply asks them, she emphasized, to comply with the same rules as everyone else.

One of the major points of contention at Tuesday’s argument was the significance of the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction. The case was the third in a trilogy of decisions on the availability of public funding for religious institutions. In Carson, the majority applied strict scrutiny – the toughest constitutional test – after it concluded that the Maine law barred some private schools from receiving public funds “solely because they are religious.”

In response to a question from Justice Clarence Thomas about whether a ruling for the challengers would require the court to extend its ruling in Carson, Reaves responded that it would not. In Carson, he insisted, the court’s “focus … was to look at … what is happening to the religious believer?” The court in Carson, he said, “didn’t focus on the text of the law in Maine. It focused on whether schools are being excluded on account of their religious exercise.”

Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Reaves on that point, observing that the law at issue in Carson specifically discriminated against religious schools – which, Roberts suggested, is not the case with the Colorado program.

Reaves pushed back. He noted that the laws in other cases involving public benefits had been neutral, rather than discriminating against religious people or organizations – for example, the court’s 1963 decision in Sherbert v. Verner, reversing a ruling by the South Carolina Supreme Court that had rejected a constitutional challenge to the denial of employment benefits from a Seventh-day Adventist whose religion barred her from working on Saturday.

Roberts later questioned Norton on a related point, asking her to differentiate the Colorado program from the law at issue in Carson and telling her that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here.” He also told Norton that the state was trying to “bury Sherbert” even though “nothing in our precedent has backed away from” it.

Two of the court’s Democratic appointees, however, echoed Roberts’ initial skepticism that Carson dictated the outcome of the challengers’ case. Justice Elena Kagan told Reaves that the trilogy of cases culminating in Carson involved laws that had excluded religious institutions and schools because of their religion. “[I]t was a nondiscrimination principle,” she emphasized, but “you’re asking us to” issue a decision that would go “far beyond” its earlier cases. In particular, she suggested, the challengers were seeking a ruling that religious people “need a special accommodation” because of their faith.

Reaves responded that an interpretation of the court’s decision in Carson that focused on whether the law at issue expressly discriminated against religion would be “very easy to circumvent.”

Kagan responded that this isn’t “a good case to raise the kind of specter of circumvention.” “[T]his is a case,” she continued, “of a state trying to enforce its own nondiscrimination principles.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to agree. She characterized Carson as a case that prohibited governments from treating religious schools worse than it treated secular schools. That doctrine, she posited, was “pretty narrow” and made “perfect sense.” But, she told Reaves, “your schools want to discriminate by exclusion” when no other school participating in the universal preschool program does so.

Some of the court’s Republican appointees were more persuaded by the challengers’ argument – also advanced by Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the challengers – that Carson should apply even if the Colorado law does not specifically target religion.

Justice Neil Gorsuch, for example, asked “what would be left” of cases like Sherbert “if everything turned on express discrimination” against religion, while Justice Samuel Alito appeared dubious that the legislators who enacted the Colorado universal preschool law “would not understand what the effect of” the law’s requirements “would be.”

Similarly, Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Norton why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows “schools will be unable to agree to?” Barrett pointed to a New York Times op-ed written in the wake of Carson by law professor Aaron Tang, who she stated suggested that states counteract some of the effects of Carson by enacting nondiscrimination requirements.

Norton resisted any effort to link Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement to an intent to target religious schools, stressing that there was no evidence of the legislature’s motives and (in response to a question from Jackson) that the requirement predated the inclusion of religious schools in the program.

The justices and advocates also debated, although less extensively than the significance of Carson, whether Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that are subject to a less stringent constitutional test, known as rational-basis review.

Reaves told the justices that the Colorado nondiscrimination requirement was not the kind of “across-the-board” prohibition that the court envisioned in Smith because the Colorado law contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catch-all” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation. Moreover, he added, the law also creates exceptions to accommodate children with disabilities and children from low-income families.

For her part, Norton characterized the preferences as very different from the kind of exclusion that the challengers seek. Even if a school receives a preference, she stressed, it is still subject to the nondiscrimination requirement.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh appeared to approach the case from what he regarded as a practical angle, asking Norton why the state wouldn’t “seek the win/win?” With over 2,000 preschools participating in the Colorado program, he said, there should be “plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers” and, at the same time, “the ability of LGBT parents” to find a school that is a good fit for their families. “Why,” he asked, “has this been provoked?”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor took a different tack, suggesting that a ruling for the challengers could have broader implications. A Catholic preschool, she told Reaves, could reject a child “merely” because his or her parents are LGBTQ. Would this, she queried, also allow a religious preschool to turn down Black children?

Reaves said that it would not. He pointed to a 1983 case in which the Supreme Court, applying strict scrutiny, upheld the Internal Revenue Service’s decision to revoke the tax-exempt status of a private university and private school with racially discriminatory admissions policies. The government in that case, he emphasized, indicated that its interest in prohibiting such policies was not merely “compelling” (the first factor under strict scrutiny) but “overriding.”

He told the justices that strict scrutiny should similarly apply to this case. “And then the government can come forward and say we have a really good reason for” excluding Catholic preschools from the program. But, he concluded, “we just don’t think they’ve done that in this case.”

By the end of the argument, Sotomayor seemed to leave little doubt about where she stood. “No matter what line of cases we follow,” she said, “there will be tremendous problems and a great cost to someone.”

A decision is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7701. Stephanie Wrobel on the nuance of twists in thrillers

Years ago, I wrote about nine types of thriller twists for CrimeReads. I spent so much time thinking about that taxonomy that it found its way into my new novel, Revenge Plot: one of my characters, a bestselling thriller writer, reflects on those twists as she develops her book.

But after writing four thrillers, and reading hundreds more, I’ve realized my taxonomy needs an addendum: not everything you figure out before the author tells you is a twist.

First, a refresher on what a twist it. I define it as a revelation that forces the reader to substantially reinterpret what came before. It is not confirmation of something the reader has been encouraged to suspect, nor the answer to a mystery that the novel has supplied enough evidence for the reader to solve. I would call these reveals.

Let’s use Gone Girl as an example, since it’s arguably the most popular thriller of the twenty-first century. Spoilers ahead! Nick’s affair with Andie is a reveal. Nick’s lies to the police are reveals. The book’s twist is that Amy staged her disappearance, fabricated the diary and evidence, and constructed a murder case against Nick.

A reveal gives the reader new information that answers a question or changes what we know. A twist changes the meaning of what we thought we knew. Gillian Flynn gives us clues that Nick is hiding something, so when we find out he’s having an affair and lying to the police, these developments confirm our suspicions of him. But at the point when we find out the diary is fabricated, we believe Amy to be the victim of this story and Nick to be the perpetrator. Finding out Amy is framing Nick forces us to reinterpret everything that came before.

Okay, so why am I being such a pedant about terminology? Because our genre’s overemphasis on twists is ruining one of the key pleasures of thrillers: deduction.

Lots of readers choose mysteries and suspense novels so they can put the clues together, then solve the crimes themselves. Sometimes we want you to say, Holy shit, what?! But other times we want you to think, I knew it! Or, Oh, of course! A good thriller should make the reader feel smart. Thriller writers plant breadcrumbs over the course of three or four hundred pages in the hope that readers will pick up on some or all of them and put the puzzle pieces together.

Our job is not to keep you from figuring anything out. It’s to control what you figure out, and when.

Alfred Hitchcock famously illustrated the distinction between surprise and suspense with his “bomb under the table” scenario. If two people are talking and a bomb suddenly explodes beneath them, the audience is surprised. Tell the audience beforehand that the bomb is there while leaving the characters oblivious, and the same scene is suspenseful. In other words, sometimes giving the audience more information is the key to making a story work.

Thriller writers constantly make versions of this choice. Sometimes I want the reader to know something my protagonist doesn’t. Sometimes I want you to suspect something but not have enough evidence to be sure. Sometimes I want you and the protagonist to arrive at the answer together. And sometimes I want you to be confidently, spectacularly wrong.

All of those experiences require the author to manage the distance between what the reader knows, what the characters know, and what the reader thinks she knows. If I’ve spent a hundred pages planting clues that Character A is secretly Character B, then you figuring out their identity on page three hundred and fifty may not mean you’ve outsmarted me. It may mean I’ve done my job.

That isn’t to say predictability is never a problem. If I intend to stun you on page three hundred yet you figure out my big twist on page thirty, something went awry. But “I guessed it” doesn’t tell us whether that happened. The more useful question is: were you supposed to be able to guess it? And when?

In our obsession with avoiding predictability, I worry that thriller writers are being pushed toward a different—and in my opinion, worse—problem: the supposedly “unguessable” twist.

Surprise alone is easy. I could reveal on the final page of my novel that a murderer was a previously unmentioned identical twin. You probably wouldn’t have guessed it, but you also might want to chuck my book across the room.

The best twists don’t merely make us say, I never saw that coming. They make us say, How did I not see that coming? Once the truth is revealed, we should be able to look backward and recognize that the clues were there all along. The author showed us the pieces; we assembled the puzzle incorrectly.

Which means “unguessable” is a strange standard to aspire to. So many reviews these days focus on whether the reader guessed the twist. (I’m guilty of this too!) So many blurbs on book covers promise one you’ll never see coming. But when every thriller is judged according to how thoroughly it fooled us, we flatten a genre capable of producing far more complicated pleasures.

We’re supposed to notice the suspicious alibi. Remember the odd detail from chapter three. Wonder why the author chose that particular word. Form theories, discard them, resurrect them fifty pages later. We’re supposed to be right sometimes.

To judge a book’s success by whether you guessed the twist early—never mind whether that “twist” was actually a reveal—is like judging a roller coaster by whether you could see the big drop coming.

Sometimes seeing it coming is half the fun.

Stephanie Wrobel grew up in Chicago but has been living in the UK for the last three years with her husband and dog, Moose Barkwinkle. She has an MFA from Emerson College and has had short fiction published in Bellevue Literary Review. Before turning to fiction, she worked as a creative copywriter at various advertising agencies. Her new book, Darling Rose Gold is now available from Berkley Books.

Justice Thomas Johnson was born on this day in 1732. As we noted in a Closer Look about Johnson in July, he has the distinction of holding the third-shortest tenure of any associate justice in Supreme Court history.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

Today, the justices will hear argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

On Friday, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

#7696. Carter Wilson on justice, manipulation, and why revenge thrillers are so satisfying

I love a revenge thriller! Someone gets horribly wronged, the people who are supposed to help prove useless, and eventually the wronged person decides, screw it, I’ll handle this myself. Things often get bloody from there. Count me in.

We all love justice served when the systems supposed to deliver it have failed. How many of us have felt purely homicidal after getting lost in an insurance company’s endless phone menu? You’ve entered your policy number four times, explained your problem to three people, and been transferred to a department that may or may not exist. Meanwhile, a recording keeps assuring you that your call is important.

Important to whom? Certainly not whoever just disconnected me.

Sure, a bureaucratic phone tree isn’t (usually) justification for a killing spree. But that feeling of powerlessness is familiar. Someone else controls the outcome, and you can’t even get them on the goddamn phone. A revenge thriller transfers power from the system to the individual. The person who’s been ignored or screwed over gets to decide what happens next.

I’ll readily admit there’s emotional manipulation involved. Give readers someone to care about and a good enough reason to want payback, and suddenly they’re willing to entertain all sorts of behavior. This works in David-versus-Goliath stories, too. Show me a corporation knowingly poisoning a town’s drinking water, and I’m probably going to be pretty flexible about what happens to its CEO in chapter thirty. This includes graphic limb removal.

Dexter takes this flexibility to impressive lengths. His code gives us permission to root for a serial killer. We know whom he’s targeting and why, and that’s enough to get us on board. Murder remains bad, of course. We’d just appreciate it if he could finish this particular one before anyone interrupts.

Victoria Helen Stone’s Jane Doe gives us a different kind of payback. Jane makes herself into the perfect girlfriend for a man she intends to destroy. He thinks he understands who she is, while the reader knows how badly he’s miscalculated. There’s something wonderful about watching a man remain so confident while getting everything so wrong. By all means, buddy, keep underestimating her.

But writing about revenge makes me consider what I’d actually do if something terrible happened to me or someone I loved. I get to explore those thoughts while sitting safely in a coffee shop with my laptop. Sometimes I don’t particularly like the answer. Sometimes I love it.

We have laws telling us what’s allowed. We have society telling us what’s acceptable. Then we have our own private understanding of good and evil, which may come with a few footnotes. Don’t hurt people. Don’t kill people. Unless, perhaps, those people are threatening your child.

That last one can do a lot of damage to an otherwise sound moral philosophy.

When I was writing When They Find Me, I never had trouble rooting for Annie Wolfe. She’s hiding with her twelve-year-old daughter, Coral, in a remote Colorado town, all because she took matters into her own hands four years ago and a couple thousand miles away. She knows her vengeance comes with a cost, and she’s waiting to be hunted down. She’s peppered her cabin with hidden weapons and built a safe room.

Then a father and his two adult children invade Annie’s house believing someone else lives there, and a historic blizzard traps everyone inside. This is bad news for Annie and Coral. It’s also an unfortunate development for the people who picked this particular cabin.

Annie will do anything to protect her daughter. I wasn’t sitting at my laptop wishing she’d consider a more measured response while armed strangers threatened them. I wanted her to have easy access to a pickaxe and a flamethrower. But Annie isn’t enjoying any of this. She just wants herself and her daughter to survive. Mostly, she just wants everyone to leave her the hell alone.

Her history with revenge is complicated, and I’ll leave the specifics for readers to discover. Annie believes in an eye for an eye. She has her own sense of proportion, and she isn’t interested in drawing out someone’s suffering. I understood her reasoning even as I wrote about the consequences.

Then there’s Coyote, the father leading the home invasion. He sees himself almost as an animal, acting according to instinct. In his belief system, nature doesn’t concern itself with good and evil. He isn’t waking up, stretching, and wondering how much bad shit he can squeeze in before lunch. He’s doing what comes to him naturally, and I had to take that posture seriously while writing him, even while I wanted Annie cave in his skull.

So there I was, drinking coffee and deciding who deserved to die. Maybe my favorite part of being a thriller writer.

I think revenge stories satisfy the part of us that’s tired of waiting for someone else to fix things. Writing them also makes me question how far I’d go once I stopped waiting. I can believe in the law and still find myself enthusiastically supporting a character who breaks it. Put my own family at risk, and who knows what I’d be willing to justify?

Fortunately, when I finish the book, the rules still apply. I have to behave like a reasonably civilized person. Which I fully intend to do.

Unless my insurance company transfers me one more fucking time.

Carter Wilson is the USA Today and Publishers Weekly bestselling author of eleven standalone psychological thrillers. His stories focus on ordinary people pushed into situations where survival and morality collide, and every decision has consequences. His 2025 novel Tell Me What You Did was a national monthly pick by Barnes & Noble, and his work has been optioned for film and television. He hosts the podcast Making It Up, where he has candid, unscripted conversations with fellow authors about what it actually takes to build a writing life. He also founded Unbound Writer, where he works closely with writers through coaching, immersive retreats, and live workshops. A sought-after speaker and moderator, Carter is known for conversations that feel honest, engaging, and a little unpredictable. He lives in Erie, Colorado and travels frequently to teach, interview, and speak. To learn more, please visit www.carterwilson.com
