#7650. DOJ steps up its investigation into the Dobbs leak

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

This week, during the first half of the November argument session, the justices heard oral arguments in four cases and quickly declined a request from the Trump administration to intervene in a voting dispute in California. However, headlines about these developments were overshadowed by Tuesday’s midterm elections. The blue wave brought new significance to debates over court reform and when Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas might retire.

Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied two requests for a stay of execution from Jesse Guardado, who was sentenced to death for the 2004 murder of Jackie Malone. Hours later, Guardado was executed in Florida.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review. Here is the link to our Case Preview.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

On Monday, the justices heard argument in Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

The justices also heard argument on Monday in Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

Monday morning, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by individuals who it contends are noncitizens. Just hours later, the court denied the request. There were no noted dissents.

Later on Monday, the court released its calendar for the January argument session, which will begin on Monday, Jan. 11.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the court to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request has been fully briefed since last Friday, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Looking ahead, the justices will hear arguments on Monday in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

Jodi Kantor and Michael S. Schmidt, The New York Times

In May 2022, Politico released a leaked draft of the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned the right to abortion. The leak was “a seismic breach of confidentiality” and led to “an internal inquiry by the court,” although “no leaker has ever been publicly identified.” But The New York Times reported on Thursday that the Justice Department is now “pursuing a criminal investigation into who leaked” the draft opinion and that this “investigation has ramped up in recent weeks as prosecutors have sent grand jury subpoenas for testimony and sought information from people who worked at the court at the time of the leaks.”

On Thursday, defenders of “a Cook County, Illinois, ordinance that makes it unlawful to sell or possess any ‘assault weapon or large capacity magazine,’ including AR-15 rifles,” asked the Supreme Court to dismiss a challenge to the ban that’s set to be argued in December, Viramontes v. Cook County. Attorneys for Cook County contended that the case is now moot after the “lead plaintiff, Cutberto Viramontes, asked [on Oct. 29] to be removed from the litigation without explanation.” Although the filings represent “a puzzling twist” in the case, “whether Viramontes is permitted to withdraw would have limited practical significance for the broad question of whether state and local governments may ban AR-15-style rifles,” according to CNN. That’s because Viramontes was consolidated with another case on a similar law in Connecticut, “which would continue even if the Supreme Court decided to dismiss the Cook County litigation. And whatever the court decides on Connecticut’s ban would almost certainly affect whether other bans like the one in Cook County can stand.”

Tuesday’s midterm elections “all but guaranteed” President Donald Trump won’t be able to put a fourth justice on the Supreme Court. Beginning in January, Democrats will have “a Senate majority—with a several-seat cushion—that will make it easy to block Trump judicial nominees, especially for any Supreme Court vacancies that might arise in 2027 or 2028,” according to The Wall Street Journal. Faced with this reality, “[s]ome legal observers have floated a last-ditch scenario in which [Clarence] Thomas or [Samuel] Alito could announce their retirement in the coming days and give Trump and the outgoing Republican Senate a chance to quickly install a successor before the newly elected Congress is seated on Jan. 3.” But the Journal described this scenario as “exceedingly unlikely,” in large part because neither Alito nor Thomas appears interested in retiring. And it’s not “clear that a Supreme Court nominee could get through the lame-duck Congress even if there were a retirement, especially because some moderate Republican senators are on their way out of office and blame Trump for losing their seats.”

In a Thursday interview with the Associated Press, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said “that Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put ‘a right-winger’ on the Supreme Court once they take power.” He “would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. But he said that Democrats are ‘not going to allow any crappy nominees’ to be confirmed to the Supreme Court.” “The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer said.

In a column for Bloomberg, Noah Feldman contended that Tuesday’s election results “should cause Democrats to reconsider the wisdom of plans to pack the court or strip it of jurisdiction over certain issues.” It should no longer feel as urgent to make such changes, according to Feldman, because “[i]f a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028 and the Democrats hold the Senate, the Democrats will have a chance to flip the court from 6-3 conservative to 5-4 liberal” simply by filling predicted or expected vacancies. The reform proposals floated in recent months “make little sense if Democrats take seriously the prospect of a liberal recapture of the institution,” Feldman wrote.

The Supreme Court heard argument on Monday in Maxwell v. Dinis on whether a federal inmate may use a habeas statute to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem: Does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers?

In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman offered an in-depth analysis of Justice Elena Kagan, examining not only how she votes, but also how she chooses to agree and disagree.

In her Ratio Decidendi column, Stephanie Barclay revisited Tuesday’s argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, noting that the discussion put a spotlight on 1990’s Employment Division v. Smith, a controversial ruling that made it easier for the government to overcome free exercise challenges. The ruling in St. Mary, according to Barclay, “will determine how much is left of” Smith, which has already fallen out of favor with the court.

In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored four petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices at today’s conference. Three concern a long-running dispute over Alabama’s congressional districts and the fourth asks whether using a car makes an otherwise local kidnapping a federal crime – even when the car never crosses a state line.

In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky explored Nielsen v. Watanabe, in which the court is considering under what circumstances federal officers may be sued for money damages for constitutional violations, noting that the case comes at a time when efforts “to hold ICE agents accountable” have taken on new urgency.

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on race and school admissions. In his AV Ristorante column on Monday, Brian Fitzpatrick explained why he believes “it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.”

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the Texas Supreme Court’s blue wave, the possibility of a majority-Democrat Supreme Court, and one of the biggest Supreme Court cases of the term: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice Peter V. Daniel, who served on the court from 1841/2 to 1860.

Like some of the other justices we’ve covered, Justice Peter V. Daniel is one that “[f]ew recall or have ever heard of.” Those who know of Daniel have not been complimentary. He has been called “a brooding proslavery fanatic” according to law professor Earl Maltz, and a 1965 book review likened him to the notoriously bigoted Justice James C. McReynolds, minus McReynolds’ occasional “charm.”

Daniel was born in April 1784 on his family’s estate in Stafford County, Virginia. After studying with private tutors and a brief stint at the College of New Jersey (now Princeton University), he read law in Richmond under Edmund Randolph, President George Washington’s attorney general and secretary of state. In 1810, Daniel married Randolph’s daughter, Lucy.

In November 1808, Daniel fought a duel in Maryland against businessman John Seddon; Seddon later died from his injuries. This did not appear to significantly slow Daniel’s career, however: He subsequently spent two one-year terms in the Virginia House of Delegates, a tenure his biographer, John P. Frank, judged as “utterly undistinguished.” In 1812, Daniel joined Virginia’s Council of State, which advised the governor, and from 1818 to 1835 served as lieutenant governor. His “friends” “apparently lacked any real warmth or affection for him, complaining of his ‘frozen deportment,’” which played out literally: In the winter of 1813, Daniel reportedly balked at spending a modest sum to keep militiamen warm, despite their officer’s warning that the men’s lives were at stake, on the reasoning that Virginia state law made the soldiers responsible for their own clothing.

Daniel’s Richmond law practice was modestly successful, but he had other aspirations. Through the Richmond Junto (a Virginia Democratic-Republican network) he organized and led the state’s Jacksonians, and, along with then-New York governor Martin Van Buren, built an “Albany-Richmond axis,” which backed Andrew Jackson for president. Daniel subsequently turned down Jackson’s offer of attorney general. In 1836, however, he accepted a federal judgeship in eastern Virginia, Jackson’s reward for his party loyalty and his support for the president’s war on the national bank.

When Justice Philip Barbour died in February 1841, Van Buren had roughly a week left in office and rushed to nominate Daniel to the court. Aware of Daniel’s reputation, Whig senators tried to stall the vote, at one point walking out together to leave the chamber without a quorum, while Democratic leaders searched the capital for their own absent senators. Daniel was ultimately confirmed 22-5 in a midnight vote. The exact date he took the oath is unclear; the Federal Judicial Center lists it in January 1842 “based on questionable authority,” while one biography entry has him joining the court in December 1841.

After he joined the bench, Daniel’s circuit assignment included Arkansas and Mississippi, which involved arduous trips from Washington. While circuit riding in 1851, for example, Daniel rode in a canal boat for two days to get from D.C. to Pittsburgh (and was not a fan of the other “vulgar and filthy” passengers).

On the court itself, close to one in three of Daniel’s written opinions was a dissent, and during his tenure, his solo dissents outnumbered any other justice’s by more than two to one. He fought against extending federal admiralty power to inland waters, and when the court did just that in 1852’s Genesee Chief v. Fitzhugh, Daniel was the lone dissenter. Perhaps his best-known majority opinion came in 1848’s West River Bridge Co. v. Dix, which put Daniel opposite the famed lawyer and statesman Daniel Webster. Daniel detested Webster so much that, after meeting him, he reported his hand “was actually contaminated by contact with his.” In the case, Vermont had taken over a privately chartered toll bridge, paid compensation, and opened it as a free road, but the bridge company argued that the takeover breached the contract clause of the Constitution. Writing for the majority, Daniel held that the franchise was ordinary property that the state could take through eminent domain.

Daniel, who was a slaveholder, concurred in 1842’s Prigg v. Pennsylvania, which held that the federal Fugitive Slave Act preempted Pennsylvania’s ban on recapturing formerly enslaved persons. After Van Buren joined the antislavery Free Soilers, Daniel’s friendship with him ended, and Daniel reportedly swore he would never again set foot north of Maryland (he came to blame even bad weather on the North). In Dred Scott v. Sandford, Daniel argued that freed slaves could not be citizens because they had once been held as property and that the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 (which, among many other things, had kept slavery out of land north and west of the Ohio River) was unconstitutional, thus taking a more extreme position than even Chief Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the majority opinion.

Daniel’s first wife, Lucy, died in 1847, and his second wife died in 1857 after a candle accidentally lit her clothes on fire. Daniel died in Richmond in May 1860 following a lengthy illness. In February 1861, Republican senators blocked President James Buchanan’s pick to replace him, Jeremiah Black, making the seat one of the three vacancies that President Abraham Lincoln filled in 1862. It stayed open until July 1862, when Lincoln chose Justice Samuel Miller.

In a December 1860 memorial, the attorney general said that Daniel “held the pen of a ready writer,” but “was sometimes in danger of going too directly to his purpose and treating with too much contempt the obstacles that intervened.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “We're talking about now, though.”

MR. SCHEPERS: “That – we believe that Atkins was new based off of the character of the decision in 2002 and that it remains new now.”

#7647. Democrats won control of Congress. So what does that mean for the Supreme Court?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Democrats won big in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping at least 40 seats in the House and at least seven in the Senate. Come January, the Democratic Party will control both houses of Congress, which will allow it to set policymaking priorities and play a lead role in shaping the future of the Supreme Court.

Most immediately, the power shift in the Senate will complicate (if not effectively eliminate) President Donald Trump’s ability to appoint another justice to the Supreme Court, should a vacancy arise after the new Congress is seated. The Democratic Party will have enough votes to reject a nomination – if it even allows confirmation hearings to proceed.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7646. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7645. Fourth Circuit narrows government request for journalists’ LinkedIn records

The Fourth Circuit attempted to strike a balance between the need to protect national security and the need to protect the free press.

RICHMOND, Va. (CN) â The Fourth Circuit instructed a lower court Tuesday to narrow the amount of journalists’ records LinkedIn must turn over for an investigation.

âThe government sought and received a pair of orders to aid an investigation into the leaking of highly confidential military information to an unnamed news outlet.

âA lower court first granted the government’s request for a sweeping disclosure order under the Stored Communications Act requiring LinkedIn to produce records of journalists’ messages with confidential sources. The government sought journalists’ metadata records from an 18-month period, including their conversations with sources.

âThe lower court also granted a secrecy order that prohibited LinkedIn from telling its users about the disclosure for one year. U.S. Circuit Judge Harvie Wilkinson, a Ronald Reagan appointee, ruled that the orders were too broad.

â"It is part of the audacity of the American project to believe that collective security can coexist with individual freedom," Wilkinson said. “While we respect the government’s interest in gathering information potentially relevant to the leak, neither the Stored Communications Act nor the Constitution permit the district court to approve orders that, by all apparent indications, are substantially overbroad.”

âWilkinson disagreed with the government’s argument that LinkedIn failed to identify an injury. Wilkinson reasoned that the orders may cause the platform reputational and financial harm.

â"Confidentiality of sources is the lifeblood of a free press," Wilkinson said.

âOver a billion people use LinkedIn, including 94% of American journalists, according to a 2022 Pew Research Center survey.

â"Through the aid of LinkedIn, a journalist and source can therefore find each other and exchange extensive information without ever establishing any publicly visible connection," Wilkinson said. “Without the ability to communicate privately that LinkedIn offers, that would be impossible.”

âThe court sealed many details of the investigation, including which news outlet shared the confidential information. The government described the subject article as revealing a top-secret United States military operation in a foreign country. The government’s attorney, Joshua Ferrentino, described the investigation as unusual during a September hearing.

âWilkinson denied LinkedIn’s motion to quash the disclosure order in its entirety. Wilkinson emphasized the life-and-death nature of the confidential information the news outlet shared.

“Leaks of classified materials can transmit highly sensitive information to our adversaries in areas in which stealth is essential,” Wilkinson said. “Such leaks can also place in greater danger the lives of the men and women working in covert operations to protect our country.”

âStill, Wilkinson acknowledged the role the press plays in American society.

â"When a free press reports on the operations of government, it will often be the case that reporting exposes matters that the government might wish undisclosed, either to save itself from embarrassment or because it simply prefers to have its actions unexamined," Wilkinson said. “This does not confer upon government the right to silence.”

âLinkedIn moved to narrow the secrecy order so it could inform a lawyer for the news outlet of the disclosures. A magistrate judge denied the motion to modify the orders, ruling that the Stored Communications Act allows platforms to challenge orders only on logistical grounds. The magistrate judge further ruled that the government’s request was not overbroad because it is typical that records requests encompass some records unrelated to the criminal investigation.

â"While some degree of overbreadth may be inevitable, the SCA and the Constitution require the district court to analyze the degree of overbreadth and trim the more far-fetched reaches of the government’s records request," Wilkinson said.

âAttorneys representing LinkedIn and the government did not return a request for comment. U.S. Circuit Judges Andrew Wynn, a Barack Obama appointee, and Nicole Berner, a Joe Biden appointee, concurred with Wilkinson.

#7642. The poisoned public rights doctrine and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Tuesday, Nov. 10, the court will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC. This case concerns the H-2A visa program for temporary alien immigrant workers. The issue is whether the Department of Labor’s Article II administrative law judges have the authority to collect ruinous fines from employers who violate their employment contracts with such individuals.

In early August of this year, I signed an amicus brief supporting Sun Valley Orchards along with former Attorneys General Edwin Meese III and Michael Mukasey and law professor Gary Lawson, prepared and filed by our lawyer Amit Vora. We argued that the respondent was entitled not only to a Seventh Amendment civil jury but also to an Article III federal court.

After reading the government’s opening and reply briefs by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, I stand by our argument that a DOL administrative law judge may not deprive Sun Valley of property by imposing ruinous fines for violating a contract that bound it to follow certain labor laws in employing foreign immigrant H-2A workers. Rather, Sun Valley has a Seventh Amendment right to have its claims heard by a jury if it desires to do so.

The government is obviously correct that the government has a sovereign right to control immigration into the United States under the H-2A program. It does not follow from that, however, that the government can condition the admission of foreign workers under this program on Sun Valley’s surrendering its constitutional right to have employment disputes with those workers adjudicated by Article III courts with a Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial. Constitutional rights cannot be taken away without due process of law or in violation of, for example, the First, Fourth, or Seventh amendments. But that is exactly what the government is trying to do in this case.

By way of example, in 1987’s Nollan v. California Coastal Commission, the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia, held that the California Coastal Commission could not use its plenary power over zoning to condition a renovation construction permit on the Nolans ceding a public easement to walk along their valuable California coastal property, as doing so would violate the takings clause of the Fifth Amendment. Likewise, the government cannot impose unconstitutional conditions when using either its zoning power or its plenary power over immigration. Nor can the government use its commerce power or any of its other enumerated powers to violate one’s constitutional rights. The government can shut down the foreign immigrant H2A program. But it cannot use it as a cudgel to make Americans surrender their constitutional rights simply because the rights of immigrants are at stake.

Central to the government’s argument otherwise is the public-rights doctrine. This doctrine – properly understood – allows for privileges created by the government to be adjudicated by non-Article III judges, such as the privileges to receive social-security, disability, or welfare payments; the privilege to immigrate into the United States; or the privilege to receive tax rebates under the federal government’s partial waiver of sovereign immunity. With regard to such privileges, the Constitution’s guarantee of an Article III forum and the Seventh Amendment civil jury trial right are inapplicable because the receipt of these were not property rights recognized at common law, but privileges created by the government. The government argues that because immigration into the country is also a privilege, not a right, Sun Valley’s conduct related to this are not subject to Article III protections.

It is true that the public rights doctrine was profoundly altered (one could say poisoned), in the 1977 case of Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety and Health Administration. In Atlas Roofing, Justice Byron White denied access to an Article III court and a Seventh Amendment civil jury trial to a party subject to an OSHA enforcement order. According to White, because such orders were based on “new statutory obligations,” they could be “committed exclusively to an administrative agency [for] deciding whether a violation has in fact occurred.” This was incorrect: while OSHA created new torts that can occur in the workplace, these were analogous to the kinds of tort actions that would have been heard at common law. Indeed, such torts are classic “Cases in Law,” which Article III gives sole jurisdiction over to life-tenured federal judges assisted by a civil jury if the plaintiffs choose one. Thus, Atlas Roofing Co. changed the law to say that the public-rights doctrine not only allowed Article II administrative law judges to deprive persons of privileges, but, for the first time, it also eliminated the guarantee of a Seventh Amendment jury trial when a person or entity was deprived of property rights by the government.

Fortunately, this dangerous precedent was limited by the more recent 2024 case of SEC v. Jarkesy. In Jarkesy, the Supreme Court held that when the SEC imposed civil penalties against a defendant for securities fraud, the Seventh Amendment entitled the defendant to a jury trial. This is because in 1787 a fraud case, like the employment contract case at issue in Sun Valley (or, for that matter, the property seized in Atlas Roofing), would have been “Case in Law” assigned to the sole jurisdiction of the Article III courts.

So the lesson of Jarkesy is this: While the vast majority of cases which ALJs decide only “privileges” and not “rights” only require an Article II hearing, when federal regulatory agencies impose ruinous fines on a corporation or person, those fines are deprivations of one’s right to property. And in depriving one of such property, it is not enough to have an administrative hearing: The case must be heard by an Article III court with the right to a Seventh Amendment civil-jury trial.

The public-rights doctrine then does not apply to enforcement orders that deprive a person of property by agencies such as OSHA in Atlas Roofing, the SEC in Jarkesy, or the DOL in Sun Valley. Nor does calling a case an immigration matter empower the government to take away the constitutional rights of Americans even if immigration into the United States is itself a privilege and not a right.

So let’s hope that the Supreme Court in Sun Valley rejects, as unconstitutional, the DOL’s attempt to funnel a private-rights dispute away from an Article III forum. And let’s further hope that the court clearly reframes the public-rights doctrine, as limited in Jarkesy, as a mere manifestation of the rights/privileges distinction – and continues to prevent the doctrine from taking the form that Justice White allowed for in Atlas Roofing: an ominous threat to Article III, the Seventh Amendment, and the due process clause.

Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

#7640. Justices consider when a constitutional rule is “previously unavailable” to prisoner

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about whether a Texas man on death row can bring a second federal post-conviction challenge to his sentence by arguing that, under updated psychiatric standards, he was found intellectually disabled and therefore cannot be executed.

Except in a few narrow circumstances, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 bars prisoners from filing a petition for federal post-conviction relief challenging the grounds for their detention when an earlier petition has already been rejected. One of these exceptions is when such a claim relies on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The other is if facts “underlying the [initial] claim” would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable fact finder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

In 2007, Dexter Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. Five years before his conviction, the Supreme Court held in Atkins v. Virginia that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment. A defense expert at Johnson’s trial concluded that, under the diagnostic standards employed at the time, Johnson was not intellectually disabled. Following his conviction, Johnson filed an initial habeas petition and invoked Atkins to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.

In May 2013, while Johnson’s first federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the DSM-5, a new edition of its diagnostic manual that deemphasized IQ cutoffs. Texas’ highest criminal court adopted this in 2018. In 2019, Johnson scored 70 on an IQ test, and an expert concluded he met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability. Johnson then filed a successive habeas challenge in the district court claiming that he could not be executed under Atkins. The trial court subsequently ruled that his claim (based on the later diagnostic criteria) had been “previously unavailable,” and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed that decision. The 5th Circuit denied rehearing, and Texas came to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

At oral argument, Texas Solicitor General William Peterson told the justices that Congress “chose to allow new claims in these applications only in limited circumstances that do not include changes in the diagnostic standards for intellectual disability.” There is no “new rule” “previously unavailable” here, because Atkins was decided before Johnson “even committed his crimes,” Peterson said.

Justice Elena Kagan pressed Peterson on why the DSM “isn’t … part of the law?” She suggested that the DSM-5 effectively created “a kind of Atkins I and an Atkins II” – first, a rule barring the execution of people with intellectual disabilities, followed by a “substantive standard” defining what it means to be intellectually disabled. Kagan later described the Atkins standard as akin to a rule with a “big gap in it” where “the DSM comes and plugs it in and it becomes part of the legal standard.”

The justices further debated what it means for a rule to be “available.” Kagan suggested, based on prior precedent, that something is “not available to you” if it makes you “run into a brick wall.” “[I]f I was going to be [previously] laughed out of court,” she said, “then, really, the rule was unavailable to me.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told Peterson that, as she understood AEDPA, Congress’ “policy choice was to give individuals one clear shot at bringing their constitutional claims.” Under Texas’ interpretation, she said, “Mr. Johnson will never get that opportunity,” which “seems like a really incongruous consequence.”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for her part, suggested that the outcome should turn on something like ripeness (whether a case is sufficiently developed for a court to decide). As she remarked to Peterson, “[i]f what we have said under Atkins is you cannot execute someone who is mentally ill, we have a certain way of determining that, and it doesn't become ripe until the DM-5 makes it ripe.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked Peterson whether the court “could resolve this case solely on the new rule issue without addressing ‘previously unavailable.’” Peterson said it could, but that Texas was asking the court to decide the “previously unavailable” question.

On behalf of Johnson, Jeremy Schepers told the justices that “existence and availability aren’t the same thing.” Atkins existed, but Johnson’s claim – based on the change in diagnostic criteria – was not previously available. When the clinical standards for intellectual disability change, Schepers argued, “the Eighth Amendment’s protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time.”

Justice Clarence Thomas was skeptical, asking, “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?” Schepers responded that Atkins “remains new now.” “What about Marbury v. Madison?” Thomas responded. Justice Amy Coney Barrett noted that when “Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, that was new.” But “I don't think anybody would describe the telephone as new today.”

Kavanaugh pointed Schepers to a “friend of the court” brief filed by Louisiana and 21 other states, which argued that because the medical standards are “constantly evolving,” Johnson’s position is “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality.” Schepers said that was incorrect, because a state prisoner gets “one opportunity to raise any claim,” and “so a prisoner could not raise a second Atkins claim.”

At one point, Justice Samuel Alito asked about a future edition of the DSM that “makes smaller changes” that “provide a greater opportunity for success.” Schepers said that claim would fail under the 5th Circuit’s reading, because “[i]t’s only a question of whether the claim had a possibility of merit before.”

Emily Ferguson, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued as a “friend of the court” in support of Texas, emphasized that it is “difficult to imagine Congress enacting a law that would allow the American Psychiatric Association, without independent action of this Court, to create a new rule of constitutional law.” She also noted that the court had made clear “states would be responsible for the method of determining intellectual disability,” and it would then make little “sense for there to be an available successive application anytime the relevant state had a new … supreme court case … or even a state lower court case that changed the framework that the state was using.”

Alito asked Ferguson whether the “Atkins rule” was “that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that is regarded as such by medical professionals,” or if “it is that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that can't be justified by the recognized purposes of punishment,” for which “the DSM would be evidence but not part of the standard itself?” Ferguson responded that the “latter formulation captures what … the Atkins Eighth Amendment rule was.”

Perhaps the most noticeable takeaway from oral argument was how subdued the justices were. The chief justice did not ask any questions, and no justice appeared to take up Johnson’s request in his brief that the court dismiss the case as improvidently granted (that is, decide that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and not resolve it), as the court did last term in Hamm v. Smith, another Atkins case.

A decision is expected by late June but is likely to come earlier.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7636. Supreme Court agrees to weigh in on Goldman Sachs arbitration dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Friday afternoon added a new case to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, granting a petition for review filed by Goldman Sachs Bank in a case over whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The dispute in which the justices agreed to weigh in, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, began three years ago, when Rhea Brown and Gregory Maze filed for bankruptcy. Both listed credit card debts with Goldman Sachs Bank as one of their debts.

The Bankruptcy Code imposes an automatic stay, which (among other things) bars creditors from attempting to collect debts from someone who has filed for bankruptcy. Because Goldman Sachs, according to Maze and Brown, repeatedly continued to try to seek payment of their credit card debts, they filed an adversary proceeding (that is, a separate lawsuit within the broader bankruptcy case) against the bank, in which they contended that the bank had willfully violated the automatic stay provision.

Pointing to an arbitration clause in their credit card agreements, Goldman Sachs asked the bankruptcy court to put the adversary proceeding on hold and require Brown and Maze to arbitrate their dispute. The bankruptcy court denied that request, and both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the 4th Circuit concluded that requiring Brown and Maze to arbitrate their claim “would interfere and conflict with the strong and established policies and purposes of the Bankruptcy Code.”

Goldman Sachs came to the Supreme Court in June, asking the justices to take up its case. It told the court that the 4th Circuit’s ruling squarely conflicted with a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. Moreover, it added, “[t]he practical stakes of these issues are enormous” because of the ubiquity of arbitration clauses in consumer credit agreements. The 4th Circuit’s decision, it said, “imperils the enforceability of arbitration agreements in many of them.”

After considering Goldman Sachs’ petition for review at four consecutive conferences, the justices granted it on Friday afternoon. The case likely will be argued sometime next year, with a decision to follow by late June or early July.

More orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday are expected at 9:30 a.m. EST on Monday.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7635. LA County Judge Robert Draper removed for willful misconduct

The California Commission on Judicial Performance cited, among other instances of misconduct, the judge's rambling discourse on race relations and Black football players when a Black attorney made her first appearance before him.

LOS ANGELES (CN) â The California Commission on Judicial Performance on Tuesday ordered Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Robert Draper removed from office for numerous counts of misconduct, including making inappropriate racial and sexual comments.

“Judge Draper persistently violated the standards governing judicial behavior and engaged in extensive and severe misconduct,” the commission said in a statement. “Judge Draperâs misconduct reflected either a concerning lack of familiarity with ethical precepts, or an unwillingness to conform to those precepts.”

The judge’s misconduct, the commission added, was aggravated by his refusal to accept responsibility and his lack of insight or remorse for his misconduct and its effect on others. Moreover, the commission said, Draper’s testimony during the proceedings against him showed a lack of candor.

Draper, 84, engaged in nine instances of willful misconduct, eight instances of prejudicial misconduct, and one instance of improper action, the commission said in its 87-page decision.

Among the formal charges that were examined at a 6-day evidentiary hearing this year was Draper’s conduct during a February 2023 posttrial hearing in a sexual harassment case.

A Black attorney made her first appearance for the defense at that hearing, which prompted Draper, without any apparent need, to launch into a rambling discourse about Black players on football teams and the history of race relations in the South.

While the commission found Draper’s comment on skin tone, miscegenation, Black football quarterbacks, and Lyndon Johnsonâs successful efforts to enact the Civil Rights Act were “irrelevant and gratuitous,” they didn’t rise to level of willful misconduct. They did, however, amount to conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice that brings the judicial office into disrepute.

Likewise, comments Draper made to two female attorneys in the case while in his chambers â to the extent that lawyers at his prior law firm would tell their secretaries “you better be able to fuck better than you can type,” amounted to prejudicial misconduct rather than willful misconduct.

On the other hand, the commission found that Draper’s so-called ex parte communication with another lawyer in the case, in which he falsely claimed that the commission had asked for a review his handling of the sexual harassment trial, amounted to willful misconduct.

Likewise, the commission said Draper committed willful misconduct when, after he had recused himself from the case in March 2023 but the defendants still sought his disqualification, he himself presided over the disqualification hearing and threatened to refer the attorneys who had sought his disqualification to the state bar.

“Judge Draper acted in bad faith because he had previously recused himself from the case and he knew he had no power to make further rulings,” the commission said. “His argument that he believed he was doing what the appellate court had ordered him to do is unsupported. Once a judge has recused from a case, the recusal is irrevocable and the judge has no power to take any action in the matter.”

The commission’s decision also cited other instances in which Draper had interacted in a demeaning manner with a femalepresiding judge and female court personnel, sent a group email to colleagues, retired judges, and commission staff that attached confidential juvenile dependency records with photographs of naked minors, and attached another email which included a photograph of himself taken from behind, without clothing.

An attorney who represented Draper in the proceeding didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

In his formal response to the charges filed in February, Draper said that the charges “were contrary to all credible evidence and/or taken wholly out of context.”

Draper was first appointed to the bench by California Governor Jerry Brown in 2012, and he was twice reelected to six-year terms. In June of this year, however, he lost a third reelection bid after the Los Angeles County Bar Association had rated him “not qualified” for judicial office.

#7631. Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Over the past few decades, several features of the administrative state have been subject to heated constitutional challenge. One of them is agency adjudication: the practice of resolving disputes “in-house” within administrative agencies instead of addressing these disputes directly in a court. Of late, the Supreme Court has applied a “history-and-tradition” methodology to assess the constitutionality of agency adjudication. But that methodology confronts the challenge of how to select from among multiple competing traditions the one that should carry the day. On Nov. 10, the court will hear a case, Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, that underscores the difficulties of carrying out its history-and-tradition methodology – difficulties that apply across many areas of law.

By way of background, the basic constitutional issue regarding administrative adjudication is as follows. Article III of the Constitution vests the “judicial power of the United States” in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. From the founding and onward, however, disputes that fall within the jurisdiction of Article III courts have been heard in tribunals belonging to the other federal branches, such as territorial courts, military tribunals, bankruptcy courts, magistrate judges, and most pertinent for current purposes, administrative tribunals – for instance, by administrative law judges.

Agency adjudication of, say, Social Security and veterans’ benefits claims is an integral part of the administrative state. It provides a streamlined way of handling these claims and avoids clogging up the Article III courts. Although there is usually a right to appeal administrative determinations at some point to Article III courts, these courts apply a deferential standard of review.

The question arises whether administrative adjudication is compatible with the judicial scheme laid out in Article III of the Constitution. This is a practically significant issue; agency dispute resolution has substantial effects on individuals and companies, who can face considerable fines or penalties. To what extent, then, is agency adjudication outside Article III courts justified? And what kinds of limitations should be placed on it?

In the past few decades, the Supreme Court has turned to “history and tradition” to answer these questions. History and tradition as methods of constitutional interpretation are likely most familiar from cases on hot-button social issues, such as Dobbs (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of a right to have an abortion) and Bruen (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of requiring certain types of licenses to carry firearms outside the home). But the court has also drawn on history and tradition to shape the scope of federal judicial power, in contexts ranging from Article III standing to equitable remedies. One such setting is the division of labor between Article III courts and agency adjudicative bodies.

History and tradition play a dual role in the law of adjudication outside Article III courts. This pattern was on display in the Supreme Court’s 2024 case Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy, which addressed the constitutionality of agency adjudication of certain claims involving securities fraud. First, tradition provides a justification for non-Article III (including agency) adjudication of a limited class of claims deemed to involve “public rights,” that is, matters which historically “could have been determined exclusively by [the executive and legislative] branches.” In Jarkesy, the court listed “the collection of revenue,” “immigration,” “tariffs,” “relations with Indian tribes,” “the administration of public lands,” and “the granting of public benefits such as payments to veterans, pensions, and patent rights” as members of this class of claims. Since these matters, the court explained, historically could have been adjudicated outside Article III courts, they may be heard by non-Article III tribunals today.

Second, tradition provides a reason that claims involving “private” rather than “public” rights must be brought before Article III courts instead of administrative tribunals. A hallmark of a private-rights suit that belongs before an Article III court, the Jarkesy court stated, is being “made of the stuff of the traditional actions at common law tried by the courts at Westminster in 1789.”

In Jarkesy, the court decided that the securities fraud claim at issue resembled common-law fraud, a traditional common-law claim and so a private right requiring an Article III tribunal. (The court also emphasized that the remedy the SEC was pursuing – civil penalties – was historically enforceable in courts of law; accordingly, the SEC was bringing a suit “at common law” to which the Seventh Amendment jury trial right attached. Jarkesy thus revolved substantially around the jury trial right, which is not a question directly presented in Sun Valley.)

Tradition, then, helps to demarcate the boundary between claims that must be adjudicated by Article III courts (private rights) and claims that may be resolved before other courts, including administrative agencies (public rights). But how should the court decide whether a present-day claim fits into a tradition of private rights or public rights? In particular, what should the court do when there are multiple traditions into which a present-day claim might fit?

The court’s upcoming case Sun Valley provides an example of the problem of “too many traditions.” Sun Valley involves a nonimmigrant visa program, administered jointly by the Department of Labor and the Department of Homeland Security, that permits American employers to hire foreign laborers to perform temporary or seasonal agricultural work. As a condition of participating in the program, employers agree to provide certain workplace arrangements to both foreign and domestic workers. DOL found that Sun Valley, a New Jersey farm, had failed to provide these arrangements, and the agency assessed hundreds of thousands of dollars in civil penalties and back wages against Sun Valley. Sun Valley was required to contest these penalties before an administrative law judge, with deferential review by an Article III court. Sun Valley challenged the administrative-adjudication requirement as a violation of Article III, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit agreed with Sun Valley.

In Supreme Court briefing, the government and Sun Valley both appeal to the history-and-tradition methodology of Jarkesy, but they sharply disagree about which tradition is relevant. The government emphasizes traditions related to immigration. According to the government, its enforcement action fits within two historical categories of public rights adjudication that did not require Article III courts: rights “belonging to the sovereign, such as the right to determine whether to allow aliens into the country,” and “privileges conferred by the government, such as public benefits granted under government programs.” In the government’s view, Sun Valley violated the conditions of bringing foreign workers to the United States through an immigration program that offered the farm a benefit. The pertinent tradition is hence the history of adjudicating immigration- and benefits- related claims outside Article III courts.

Sun Valley, by contrast, casts its claim as akin to common-law breach of contract – a traditional private right requiring an Article III tribunal. DOL’s allegation, Sun Valley observes, was that Sun Valley had violated its agreement to provide certain working conditions to foreign and domestic workers. That allegation, Sun Valley contends, is simply a charge that Sun Valley breached a contract. Sun Valley further argues that DOL sought common-law remedies and in particular civil penalties – more evidence that the claim at issue involves a private right. To Sun Valley, the case is located outside the historical tradition of immigration adjudication because it is based on conditions of employment rather than immigration status. Consequently, it was unconstitutional for DOL to adjudicate Sun Valley’s dispute in-house.

Which party is right about the tradition into which the dispute over Sun Valley’s working conditions falls? Plausibly, the answer is “both.” Yes, the government is alleging that Sun Valley violated an agreement; but the agreement in question was concluded as part of an immigration program allowing Sun Valley to hire foreign workers.

So what are courts to do when, as here, they are faced with “too many traditions” – that is, traditions with different implications for the constitutional question at hand?

One possible response is to conclude that history-and-tradition analysis is hopelessly indeterminate and to reject this methodology. While many methods of constitutional interpretation fail to yield a single right answer, “history and tradition” is often justified precisely by its promise to produce constraint and fixity. Breaking this promise might be viewed as grounds for abandoning the history-and-tradition approach.

Complete repudiation of history and tradition, however, would be unwarranted. Historical practice has played an important role in both upholding and limiting non-Article III adjudication; it is a tool in judges’ toolbox and should not be thrown away.

Another option is to supplement history-and-tradition methodology, when it does not produce a clear result, with other modes of constitutional analysis. Earlier cases on non-Article III adjudication, for instance, appealed openly to practical considerations of government efficiency.

A third option would be to draw on other “modalities” of constitutional interpretation to inform the choice of which strand of tradition to emphasize. One such modality is precedent. Jarkesy did not directly confront a program like the DOL’s in Sun Valley, so it is not controlling precedent. But Jarkesy did seem to treat Congress’ broad power over immigration as a reason to uphold agency adjudication in immigration-related cases. Perhaps this suggests that DOL’s enforcement action fits better into a traditional public-rights than private-rights category.

The court may also decide to avoid the problem of too many traditions by taking a statutory “out.” When it took the case, the court added a question regarding DOL’s statutory authority to impose civil penalties and back wages on Sun Valley. The court may decide that DOL lacks such statutory authority, potentially by appealing to constitutional avoidance (in other words, construing the statute to grant DOL such authority would raise serious questions about the constitutionality of agency adjudication, which should be avoided unless necessary to decide). But the statutory question is not straightforward, and resolving it may well have ramifications for a wide array of agency-imposed penalties. At any rate, one or more of the justices can be expected to opine on Article III in Sun Valley, and the Article III issue is bound to recur.

Overall, the problem of “too many traditions” is by no means unique to the context of non-Article III adjudication. The Supreme Court faces challenging questions about how to apply history-and-tradition methodology when a present-day practice could plausibly fit into multiple traditions. The court’s response to these questions may have an important impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.

Rachel Bayefsky is Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, where she writes about civil procedure, constitutional law, and legal theory. She clerked for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in the 2018-2019 Term.

Larisa Sopka and her daughters were dining at the Cheesecake Factory at Westfield Southcenter Mall in Tukwila in May 2022 when chaos erupted in the restaurant. Nearby patrons in the midst of an argument fired a gun, and the bullet struck Sopkaâs left leg.

âRowdy table behavior at The Cheesecake Factory had never in the past led to gun violence of any kind, and it was not reasonable for the staff to have anticipated that gunshots would be fired in the restaurant on the evening of May 31, 2022 in sufficient time to have prevented it or provided any earlier warning than the shout of âgunâ that occurred that night,â Rothstein, a the Jimmy Carter appointee, wrote.

But Rothstein also dismissed the claims against the security company. Under its contract with the mall, Allied Universal patrols the premise of the mall, but employees were told not to go into a tenant space unless specifically requested.

The shooting occurred inside the restaurant and the security company didnât have a contractual duty to monitor or patrol inside the Cheesecake Factory.

âThe evidence does not support a finding that Allied had any control over security for the restaurant that would create a duty to protect the plaintiffs in the restaurant from a criminal act, even if it were foreseeable,â Rothstein wrote.

There was evidence before the court of âunruly and loud behaviorâ inside the restaurant, but Rothstein found it insufficient to establish that gunfire was imminent.

âThere is no evidence that Allied assumed responsibility for the safety of The Cheesecake Factory customers, there is no evidence that Allied knew or should have known of the specific threat, even though it may have been aware of car thefts or other violent incidents that had occurred at Southcenter Mall in the past, and there is no evidence that Allied failed to respond to a call for assistance,â Rothstein wrote.

The Sopka family had claimed the mall was the site of âscores of crimes, including assaults, shootings, carjackings, robberies, thefts, and instances of domestic violenceâ since well before the May 2022 incident.

The plaintiffs contended the restaurant, security company and mall all failed to implement appropriate security protocols, noting one of the Cheesecake Factoryâs employees who worked at the location of the shooting told local news that âliterally anyone can walk in and shoot a gun. We donât have security or someone guarding the door.â

ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (CN) â A New Mexico Highlands University professor is suing the school for retaliation and discrimination, saying it placed him under investigation after he proposed a diversity, equity and inclusion initiative to his colleagues in 2025.

In his suit filed in Las Vegas District Court Tuesday, JesÃºs Antonio Rivas-Molina, a biology professor, claims disciplinary actions the university took against him violated his free speech and equal protection rights. He is asking the court to prohibit the university from enforcing or maintaining those sanctions, which include two written reprimands, removal from his position as department chair, a performance-improvement plan and a last-chance agreement.

The slew of disciplinary measures came after Rivas-Molina sent a message recommending a DEI initiative to all faculty and administration on March 27, 2025.

âIn this day and age where diversity principles are being attacked ferociously at the federal level, with so many universities caving and complying with the elimination of DEI initiatives, it is important that we double down in our commitment to promoting and supporting diversity in our university,â Rivas-Molina wrote in the message.

After faculty members claimed Rivas-Molina’s proposal was âheteronormative, misogynistic, racist and unfairly biased," acting Provost Brandon Kempner launched an investigation into him, he says in his complaint.

When Rivas-Molina learned of the external investigation in April 2025, he sent an email to a faculty association, stating he believed the accusations were retaliatory and complaining that the faculty senate, faculty association and the university were âmarching at locked step with the federal government.â Rivas-Molina later compared the criticisms of him to language white supremacist groups use when talking about DEI being racist against white people.

The university, located in Las, Vegas, New Mexico, placed him on administrative leave.

Despite university policy requiring otherwise, the school did not interview witnesses Rivas-Molina identified during the external investigation, he says in his complaint. He says he continued to push back, approaching Kempner and other university officials in August 2025 and arguing the âenforcement of different treatment against him for handbook violations was discriminatory." He claims officials then threatened to block him from using his university email.

The next month, he received his first written reprimand.

Rivas-Molina says he brought his complaints of discrimination to the faculty senate executive committee, arguing the university applied its rules differently to white faculty members and “brown people.”

Two professors on the committee then sought no-contact orders against him and reported him to Human Resources for discrimination and retaliation. Rivas says the department did not investigate his own claims of discrimination and that he instead received further punishment.

Put on probation, Rivas-Molina says the university ordered him to file a monthly report on his progress toward being “more inclusive in his communications.” He says he was eventually threatened with termination, and that the university rejected a recommendation from a New Mexico Public Employee Labor Relations Board hearing officer to rescind the initial disciplinary actions taken against him.

The biology professor, who identifies as Hispanic and is from Venezuela, claims the university discriminated against other professors, as well, saying that a professor from India left the university after it failed to investigate racist comments made by another faculty member.

The defendants include NMHUâs Board of Regents, Kempner, Kathy Jenkins, Jennifer Lindline, Brown, Lekan, Josh Hanna, Neil Woolf and 10 unnamed defendants. The case is assigned to Chief Judge Flora Gallegos, and Rivas, who is represented by attorney Eric Sirotkin, requested a 12-person jury for trial.

The parties did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

#7627. Court declines to hear dispute tied to George Floyd protests and cases involving former baseball player Roberto Clemente and actor Randy Quaid

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in over 200 cases, including a dispute that arose in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd in police custody in 2020 and clashes involving actor Randy Quaid and the sons of a baseball legend. These denials were part of a list of orders from the court’s Nov. 6 conference that was released on Monday morning.

The court on Friday granted one petition for review from that conference, in a case involving whether and when a bankruptcy court can refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The Minneapolis case was brought by a group of businesses located at the intersection where Floyd was killed. Following Floyd’s death, the city blocked the intersection “with concrete barricades,” which “prevented vehicles and pedestrians from accessing” the area, and withdrew police protection, according to the businesses’ petition for review. Those barricades remained in place “for over one year,” and led to significant economic losses for the businesses and a surge in violent crime, the petition said.

The businesses challenged the city’s actions in state court, alleging that it had violated the Constitution’s takings clause and similar protections in Minnesota’s constitution by interfering with their operations and failing to compensate them accordingly. However, a district court and the Minnesota Court of Appeals disagreed, and the Minnesota Supreme Court denied the businesses’ request for it to review the case.

In August, the businesses came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to revive their case. On Monday, the Supreme Court declined to do so without comment.

The case involving family members of baseball legend Roberto Clemente also involved the takings clause. Clemente’s adult sons and companies associated with preserving Clemente’s legacy challenged Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image on “license plates and tags,” an initiative that “generat[ed] 15 million dollars for Puerto Rico” but also fueled ill will against the family, “who Puerto Ricans thought were to blame for a fee levied on them during dire economic times,” according to the petition for review. Through their lawsuit, the Clementes aimed to block Puerto Rico from using their father’s image in the future and recover financial damages.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit prevented the Clemente family’s takings clause claim from proceeding, emphasizing that it (along with the federal statute concerning trademark law) is “designed not to protect legacies but instead to remedy ... the taking of property for public use without just compensation.” In June, the Clementes asked the Supreme Court to take up the case and, among other things, clarify that the takings clause can apply in cases involving intangible property.

After considering the petition at three consecutive conferences, the justices on Monday denied review.

In Monday’s order list, the justices also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on AstraZeneca UK Ltd. v. Atchley, a case on whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 “of the world’s largest pharmaceutical and medical-device companies” under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting terrorists in Iraq.

Additionally, the justices sent Roybal v. Griffith, a transgender female inmate’s challenge to jail policies in El Paso County, Colorado, regarding the treatment of transgender inmates back to the lower court for reconsideration in light of West Virginia v. B.P.J. and United States v. Skrmetti.

In B.P.J., the court ruled in June that state laws barring transgender female athletes from participating on women’s and girls’ sports teams do not violate a federal civil rights law or the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. In Skrmetti, the court last year upheld a Tennessee law prohibiting some medical treatments for transgender minors, holding that it was not subject to heightened scrutiny under the equal protection clause.

Also on Monday, the justices granted the solicitor general’s request to participate in three oral arguments during the December argument session:

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7626. Giving and Receiving: Adoption attorney often on road donates building to legal services group for children

Lawyers sometimes take unusual paths to the profession, but adoption lawyer Robert Noone’s was inspired by men of the cloth. After attending St. Mary’s Seminary in Baltimore, he was helping an order of Jesuits assist the residents of Appalachia with community organizing and voting issues. The priests encouraged Noone to enter law school instead of the priesthood because they thought he could better advocate for social change as an attorney.

To support himself through West Virginia University College of Law, he played guitar in bars. After graduating in 1983, he did labor law and personal injury work at Crandall & Pyles, and by 1989 he decided to open his own firm, Robert Noone Legal Services, where he represented children as a guardian ad litem in abuse and neglect cases and as a juvenile defense attorney with cases that ranged from truant kids to kids who kill. He also handled some adoption cases in West Virginia. He now focuses on adoption services in West Virginia and Alabama.

In 2024, he signed over the deed to his 5,000 square-foot building in Logan, West Virginia, and renovated the building for its new tenant. and this month, ChildLaw Services Inc.—a statewide nonprofit law firm that exclusively works with children by offering life skills and educational programs and legal help for juvenile defense, guardianships and other services—moved in. The nonprofit law firm named the building the Noone ChildLaw Center for Children and Teens.

ChildLaw helped Noone with his work over the years, and he later became a “virtual lawyer”—performing almost everything online and meeting people by video, at their homes or inside local fast-food restaurants. He plans to continue adoption work without an office.

“He has always had a love and heart for children, so we’ve teamed up over the years on projects. He’s been a good friend,” says Monica Holliday, ChildLaw Services’ executive director.

Where you really considering becoming a priest?

Yeah, let's not say that loud. I'd been in a minor seminary, then a college seminary and then getting ready to go into theology. The Catholic education back in the liberal days, they tell you to question everything. And I think I questioned myself right out of a religion. And I went to work with the Jesuits.

Why after making partner at Crandall & Pyles did you decide to start your own firm?

I had a judge tell me: “Bob, I've watched you for a while. It's time for you to, you know, venture out on your own.” And that gave me confidence. And, you know, a lot of encouragement from friends. And what I would not want to write down, though, in a labor law firm, I was probably paid less than my secretary.

Is it true you wear the hats of both an airplane pilot and the Rev. Bob Noone, officiating marriages, including same-sex weddings?

I would meet people at airports and perform them there, but also I did a lot just in my office. I wanted people to feel that it was not just a “drive-by” wedding. Or “fly-by,” as the case may be. I always made them tell me their love story, and I would shape the vows from what I learned. That was fun when the South was so resistant to change. … Now acceptance of LGBTQ has gotten better here.

You worked as a guardian ad litem during your career and then decided to just focus on the legal work around adoptions. Why?

You get to that point. Where you hear your last sad story: that mother who wouldn't see her kid because, oh, she forgot to go pee in a jar. And I hit that point a few years back, and I decided I'm just going to help put kids in homes.

You are a music lover and have been in many bands as a performer. But you have a story about a young lady who was skipping school who also, you discovered, had some hidden musical talent.

This would have been around 2009. I was doing a lot of juvenile work then, and she was truant. I said, “What do you do for fun?” And she was big. She quit going to school because she was so overweight. And she said, "Well, I love to sing." I’m thinking she would name Pink or Gwen Stefani or one of these people. She goes, “Aretha Franklin.” Well, she did great. But the real kicker was, I said, “If you go to school”—this was in like April—"the next two months without missing, you'll get to sing with my band, Daddy Rabbit."

How many adoptions have you helped with over the years?

When I count all those I supervise—I have two lawyers now that work with me—probably a little over 2,000.

In West Virginia last week, there's one point the three of us may be in four or five different counties in one day. People thought after 43 years, I'm giving a building away, I'm retiring. Hell to the no! I'm only 69, people. There's a lot of music left to play, cases to argue.

What kinds of challenges do you help navigate for people wanting to adopt?

In West Virginia, we do our same-sex adoptions, but we also do adoptions for people that aren't married. You know, just to clarify, because [the law] says a single parent can adopt or a married couple—husband and wife—but it doesn't say a single parent. And Alabama, in fact, passed a law that specifically forbids two single people from adopting. Go figure that out.
